summary: Explains attacks that are possible when an EAP peer is not protected from man-in-the-middle attacks in tunnel methods, because the existing cryptographic binding mainly protects the server. It recommends mutual cryptographic binding based on the Extended Master Session Key.

eli5.summary: A secure tunnel only helps if both ends can tell nobody sneaked in. This makes both sides prove they share the same secret.

questions: what is the eap server insertion attack
subtitle: Why EAP tunnel methods need to protect the peer as well as the server, and how EMSK-based binding does it.

tldr.problem: In EAP tunnel methods, cryptographic binding based on the inner method's MSK protects the server but not the peer, so a legitimate but untrusted NAS can insert itself and impersonate a service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes this server insertion attack, weighs mitigations, and recommends mutual cryptographic binding based on the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK), which even a legitimate NAS never learns.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational guidance: it recommends that TEAP gain EMSK-based binding, that implementations track whether mutual authentication happened, and that server naming be standardized.

today: RFC 7029 is an Informational document that no listed RFC obsoletes or updates. Its recommendations were addressed to the work then in progress on TEAP, which the text calls a Work in Progress.

sections.title: Tunnel Methods and the Classic Attack
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP, RFC 3748) authenticates a peer to an authentication server. Peers have traditionally not relied much on what the server tells them, but facilities such as channel binding (RFC 6677) now give peers information they must trust. That gives an attacker who can impersonate the EAP server more to gain.

Such facilities are being added to tunnel methods, which carry an inner authentication inside an outer tunnel. Tunnel methods must be careful about man-in-the-middle attacks. In the classic attack, an attacker impersonates the server to the peer and offers the inner method, while opening its own tunnel to the real server. The server then believes it talks to the peer, but at the outer level it is talking to the attacker.

The classic fixes are policy (do not offer the same method inside and outside a tunnel) and cryptographic binding, where the outer party proves knowledge of the inner method's Master Session Key (MSK). RFC 3748 makes the proof to the peer optional, and the RFC argues that proving MSK knowledge is not enough for the peer.
sections.eli5: Imagine passing notes through a tunnel, and a sneaky kid slips into the middle and copies your notes to the real receiver. Binding is a secret handshake that shows both ends really are the same people.

sections.title: The Server Insertion Attack
sections.content:
The RFC's example: a compromised print server, a relatively untrusted service, intercepts a user who is trying to reach a trusted financial application. Both use AAA to carry EAP back to the user's EAP server. The print server offers a tunnel to the peer, passes the inner method on to the AAA server, and claims to be the financial application. After the inner method completes, the AAA server sends the MSK to the print server. If only the MSK is needed for cryptographic binding, the print server can complete it and impersonate the application.

For the attack to work, the attacker must be able to establish a tunnel the peer will use, respond to the inner authentication (a legitimate NAS can forward it over AAA), and usually complete the tunnel method afterwards. The gains it describes include learning what the peer wants to connect to, sending information the peer trusts, and influencing session parameters. The main focus is attackers that are legitimate NASes.
sections.eli5: A dishonest shop clerk pretends to be the bank. Because the real bank hands the clerk the same key it gives anyone who serves you, the clerk can fool you.

sections.title: Mitigation Strategies
sections.content:
The RFC examines five defenses.

  • Server authentication: if the peer validates the tunnel server's certificate and identity, the attacker cannot set up the tunnel. In practice this is hard: there is no obvious name for a tunnel server, trust anchors are unclear, and many peers make validation easy to disable.
  • Server policy: the server only performs the inner authentication inside a tunnel, combined with peer policy that requires exactly one tunnel of a given type. It works only if the inner method is EAP, produces a key, and is not available through other means such as LDAP.
  • Existing cryptographic binding: server and peer both prove knowledge of the inner MSK, which is enough against attackers that are not legitimate NASes.
  • EMSK-based binding: see the next section.
  • Mixing a key into long-term credentials: mix tunnel key material into the secret behind the inner authentication. It seems the only way to strengthen non-EAP inner methods, but depends heavily on the inner method and looks like a layering violation.
sections.eli5: There are several ways to stop the sneaky kid: check who you are talking to, make rules about which doors are used, share a secret handshake, or change the lock on the inner box.

sections.title: EMSK-Based Cryptographic Binding
sections.content:
The Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) is never disclosed to any party other than the EAP server and the peer, so even a legitimate NAS cannot learn it. If the same techniques currently used with the inner MSK are applied to the inner EMSK, an attacker cannot complete the binding.

The RFC states EMSK-based cryptographic binding as a security claim that holds when:

  • The peer proves to the server that the inner and tunnel peers are the same.
  • The server proves to the peer that the inner and tunnel servers are the same.
  • The tunnel's MSK and EMSK depend on the MSK and EMSK of inner methods.
  • The peer MUST be able to force authentication to fail if it cannot confirm the server's identity.
  • The proofs stay secure even against attackers who know the inner MSK.

EMSK-based binding only works for key-deriving inner EAP methods. It is also incompatible with deployments that insert intended intermediates, since an intermediate cannot learn the EMSK. If it is optional, the negotiation of whether to use it MUST be protected by the inner MSK or EMSK.
sections.eli5: The EMSK is a secret kept only by you and the real server, never handed to anyone in between. Using it for the handshake means a middleman who only holds the ordinary key cannot fake it.

sections.title: Recommendations and Tunnel Methods Surveyed
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that the Tunnel EAP method (TEAP) gain EMSK-based cryptographic binding, and that channel-binding support added to other methods come with a binding that protects against server insertion. Implementations offering channel binding or other peer services MUST track whether mutual authentication has happened, SHOULD default to not permitting those services until it has, and SHOULD support a configuration where the peer fails unless mutual authentication takes place. It also calls for a standard way to name EAP servers in certificates, and more study of the key-mixing idea.

The survey of methods says: TEAP supports EMSK-based binding and, where EMSK is unavailable, MSK-based binding that is not sufficient for peer services. EAP-FAST (RFC 4851) provides MSK-based binding and requires server certificate validation but gives no naming guidance. EAP-TTLS (RFC 5281) does not support cryptographic binding and has no protected result indication.
sections.eli5: The advice: add the strong handshake to the newest tunnel type, keep track of whether both sides really proved themselves, and agree on how to name servers so people can check them.

cells: EMSK-based, plus MSK-based when EMSK is unavailable
